content.title: First national suicide prevention seminar
content.summary: Worldwide suicide rates have increased by 60 per cent in the past 50 years - mainly in developing countries - and for every person who commits a suicide, 20 or more may attempt suicide.

content.text: Worldwide suicide rates have increased by 60 per cent in the past 50 years - mainly in developing countries - and for every person who commits a suicide, 20 or more may attempt suicide. For family and friends affected by a suicide or attempted suicide, the emotional impact can last for many years. To raise awareness around the issue of suicides, Aga Khan University (AKU) and the Suicide Prevention and Research Interest Group (SPRInG-AKU) in collaboration with Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg School of Public Health hosted Pakistan's first national seminar on suicide prevention.

Speaking on the occasion, Dr Murad M Khan, Professor and Chair, Department of Psychiatry, AKU said that about a million people worldwide commit suicide every year and another 10 to 20 million people attempt a suicide. The World Health Organization has declared suicides and attempted suicides as major public health problems. He mentioned that Pakistan, a Muslim-majority country, used to have a low incidence of suicide but has seen a dramatic rise in cases since the mid-1990s: from a few hundred to the current estimates of 6,000 to 8,000 a year. Social factors such as poverty, unemployment, lack of social support and low education, and psychological factors such as depression have been identified as important risk factors in suicides in Pakistan. Common methods include hanging, shooting and ingesting insecticides. More men than women kill themselves but more women than men attempt suicide. The socio-cultural and religious aspects of suicide have not been sufficiently studied yet.

Dr Haider Naqvi, Assistant Professor, Psychiatry, underlined the need for more research in this area, citing examples such as assessing society's attitudes towards suicide, whether an individual's perception of his faith holds effective deterrence value, and the stigma faced by families of the suicide victim.

Suicide is also one of the three leading causes of death among young people. Dr Ehsanullah Syed, Assistant Professor, Psychiatry pointed out factors such as parental separation, divorce and family discord, child abuse and use of alcohol and drugs add to risks of young people attempting to take their lives which is not only tragic but a great loss to societies. There is a great need to introduce life skill programmes in educational institutions that can teach young people about stress management, conflict resolution and healthy living. He also underlined the crucial importance of making psychological counselling available in all educational institutions.

Research in Pakistan has shown that suicidal behaviour is high amongst young married women. Early marriages, little independence in choosing a partner, pressure to have children early in the marriage, economic dependence on husband and conflicts with in-laws, Dr Nargis Asad, Assistant Professor in the Psychiatry Department reported, all create a great deal of psychological distress which can lead to suicidal behaviour.

But under the Pakistan Penal Code both suicides and attempted suicides are considered criminal offences, punishable with a financial penalty and a jail term. Forensic medicine specialist and Assistant Professor, Department of Pathology and Microbiology Dr Zahid Bashir, highlighted that though prosecution is rare in practice, it is not uncommon for families of a suicide victim or of the survivor of an attempt to be harassed. This makes patients and their families hesitant to seek the specialist mental health treatment they may need. He called for an urgent review and repeal of the law against suicide, so people could seek help without fear of persecution by the police.

Moving to the crucial role that hospital emergency rooms play in management of suicidal patients - as this is the first point of contact after an attempt - Dr Muhammad Shahid, Senior Instructor, Department of Emergency Medicine, stressed that patients need both medical as well as psychological treatment.
